questions.prompt: A vector database's three core jobs are
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Store, search, and update vectors at scale

Storing durably, searching fast, and updating continuously are exactly what a plain in-memory list can't do at scale.
keyPoints: Storing durably, searching fast, and updating continuously are exactly what a plain in-memory list can't do at scale.

questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: What scale, update pattern, and filtering needs does the system actually have

Requirements — scale, updates, filtering, operations — should drive the choice, not popularity or recency.
keyPoints: Requirements — scale, updates, filtering, operations — should drive the choice, not popularity or recency.

questions.prompt: The right way to choose settings like ef or nprobe is to
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Benchmark recall@k and latency on a labeled evaluation set across a range of settings

A concrete, measured recall/latency curve — not intuition or defaults — is what lets you pick a setting that matches your product's actual needs.
keyPoints: A concrete, measured recall/latency curve — not intuition or defaults — is what lets you pick a setting that matches your product's actual needs.

questions.prompt: Dense embeddings tend to struggle with which kind of query?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Exact tokens like SKUs or error codes that aren't well represented semantically

Rare exact tokens like SKUs or codes often aren't captured meaningfully by embedding space geometry, which is where sparse methods help.
keyPoints: Rare exact tokens like SKUs or codes often aren't captured meaningfully by embedding space geometry, which is where sparse methods help.

questions.prompt: Sharding a vector database primarily helps you scale
questions.referenceAnswer: Sharding distributes data and load across machines, which is what lets the system grow past single-machine limits.
keyPoints: Sharding distributes data and load across machines, which is what lets the system grow past single-machine limits.

choices.text: Storage capacity and query throughput beyond what one machine can handle
The accuracy of the embedding model
The number of distance metrics available
The size of a single vector's dimensionality

questions.prompt: Which of these is a direct lever for reducing vector database storage cost?
questions.referenceAnswer: Quantization and lower dimensionality both directly shrink the memory footprint per vector, a major cost driver at scale.
keyPoints: Quantization and lower dimensionality both directly shrink the memory footprint per vector, a major cost driver at scale.

choices.text: Quantizing vectors or using lower-dimensional embeddings
Increasing the number of replicas
Adding more metadata fields to every vector
Switching to exact brute-force search

questions.prompt: The main architectural benefit of pgvector is that it
questions.referenceAnswer: Keeping vectors inside Postgres means one system and one query language instead of coordinating data across two databases.
keyPoints: Keeping vectors inside Postgres means one system and one query language instead of coordinating data across two databases.

choices.text: Lets vector search live in the same database as relational data, avoiding syncing between two separate systems
Eliminates the need for any distance metric
Only works for sparse vectors
Provides better scale than any purpose-built vector database

questions.prompt: Why is comparing a vector from an old embedding model against a vector from a new one meaningless, even though both are valid arrays of numbers?
questions.referenceAnswer: Vector spaces from different models aren't aligned, so a distance calculated across them carries no meaningful signal, regardless of array format.
keyPoints: Vector spaces from different models aren't aligned, so a distance calculated across them carries no meaningful signal, regardless of array format.

choices.text: Because different models produce vectors in geometrically unrelated spaces, so distances between them don't reflect real similarity
Because the arrays would have different lengths
Because vector databases reject vectors from more than one model
Because only integers can be compared for similarity

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Test cache isolation and cross-tenant negative cases. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Test cache isolation and cross-tenant negative cases.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.
